For example, gross national product (GNP), gross domestic product (GDP), gross national income (GNI), literacy rate, life expectancy, Human Development Index (HDI), infant mortality rate, calorie intake, doctors per person.

## Human Development Index

- The UN created the** Human Development Index (HDI)** in 1990 as a better way of measuring differences between countries
- The index takes into account **four indicators** of development:

  - **Life expectancy at birth**, indicating overall health of a country
  - **Mean years of schooling **for adults aged 25 years
  
    - It is a measure of the educational level of a population's adults
  - **Expected years of schooling **that a child of school entrance age can expect to receive
  
    - It shows how well the younger generation will do in school
  - **Gross National Income** (GNI) per capita (PPP\$)
- Countries can be divided into four groups using HDI

  - **Very High Human Development (VHHD) **
  - **High Human Development (HHD)**
  - **Medium Human Development (MHD)**
  - **Low Human Development (LHD)**
- HDI is scored from 0 to 1
- The higher the HDI, the higher the level of development and quality of life

  - Norway has the highest HDI at 0.957  (2024)
  - Niger has the lowest HDI at 0.394 (2024)

![World map coloured by data range, with regions in colours from a legend: yellow to dark red, indicating values from 0.4 to 1.0, and grey for no data.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/5692032794ce-11384-human-development-index.png)

*Human development index*

- The index only takes into account four indicators of development and the statistics provided by some countries may be unreliable and ***subjective***
- It is a general measure based on average calculations

  - It does not take into account disparities (differences) that might exist within a country
  - It does not take into account environmental or political measures
  - Some consider it still to be too simple and biased in favour of HICs, as income is weighted

title: Detailed Specific Example: Botswana (MIC)
bodyMd:
# Detailed Specific Example: Botswana (MIC)

## Specification link

This page covers section 8.3.4 of the [CIE IGCSE specification](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/718150-2027-2029-syllabus.pdf) .

- **8.3.4 **- One detailed specific example of a named country classified as an MIC or LIC, to include:

  - The reasons for its current level of development.
  - The strategies and techniques used to try to raise its level of economic development, quality of life and standard of living.

## Reasons for Botswana's level of development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_476xcWnVhmsrTb7Z` · "One detailed specific example of a named country classified as an MIC or LIC, to include:
• the reasons for its current level of development
• the strategies and techniques used to try to raise its level of economic development, quality of
life and standard of living."

## Reasons for Botswana's level of development

- Botswana is an example of how natural resources, when well-managed, can lead to sustainable development
- Through **top-down policies** (government-led investment and governance) and **bottom-up impacts** (education and health improvements for communities), it has risen to **MIC status** while maintaining environmental and social stability

### Location and background

- **Botswana** is a** landlocked country** in **Southern Africa**, bordered by South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe, and Zambia
- Population: Around **2.6 million**
- Gained independence from Britain in **1966** – has since experienced **stable governance and steady growth **
- **GDP per capita **was \$7,820 USD in 2023 and is classified as a MIC

### Reasons for Botswana’s development success

#### Natural resources – diamonds

- Botswana is one of the world’s largest producers of **gem-quality diamonds**
- Diamond revenue makes up **~80% of export earnings**
- The government formed a **joint venture with De Beers** (Debswana), ensuring a **share of profits**

#### Political stability and good governance

- One of the most stable democracies in Africa
- Low levels of corruption and **transparent budgeting**
- The country has a strong legal system and respect for property rights
- Investment in ***rule of law***** and *****institutional trust***

#### Low population pressure

- Relatively **small population** with low density
- Less strain on infrastructure and natural resources compared to other LICs in the region

## Development strategies for Botswana

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_rtZxWtwXQt53KMzT` · "One detailed specific example of a named country classified as an MIC or LIC, to include:
• the reasons for its current level of development
• the strategies and techniques used to try to raise its level of economic development, quality of
life and standard of living."

## Development strategies for Botswana

- Botswana has implemented a **range of top-down and bottom-up strategies** to improve living conditions and economic performance

#### 1. Investment in education

- Free primary education and improved access to secondary schools
- Focus on **skills development** through vocational and technical training to match labour market needs
- Aim: reduce reliance on mining and build a more **diversified economy**.

#### 2. Healthcare improvements

- One of Africa’s most effective large-scale responses to **HIV/AIDS **through

  - Free antiretroviral therapy (ART) since the early 2000s
  - Public awareness campaigns and healthcare worker training
- Improved child vaccination, maternal healthcare access and rural health clinics

#### 3. Infrastructure development

- Significant government spending on better **roads, electricity access, and water supply**, particularly to rural areas
- Investment in telecommunications to support economic diversification
- Improved **transport links** have helped develop tourism and trade

#### 4. Anti-corruption policies

- Botswana ranks highly for **government transparency** in Africa
- Competitive salaries for public officials to reduce bribery
- Legal and institutional checks on misuse of public money are done
- Institutions like the **Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime (DCEC)** play a key role

#### 5. Economic diversification

- The government has encouraged sectors beyond mining:

  - **Tourism** (e.g. Okavango Delta, safari industry)
  - **Finance** and **ICT**
- Promotion of **foreign direct investment (FDI)** in non-mining sectors

#### Why did Botswana succeed?

- Used diamond wealth **wisely and equitably**
- Invested in **people and institutions**
- Maintained **political and financial stability**
- Fought corruption effectively – unlike many of its neighbours

title: Evaluation of strategies to reduce uneven development
bodyMd:
# Evaluation of strategies to reduce uneven development

## Specification link

This page covers section 8.3.3 of the [CIE IGCSE specification](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/718150-2027-2029-syllabus.pdf) .

- **8.3.3 **- An evaluation of the strategies and techniques used to try to reduce uneven development, for example, trade, international aid, and debt relief.

## Trade and uneven development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_Xs9xfyh9dYx3Qpn4` · Social, economic, and environmental strategies and techniques used to try to achieve sustainable development.

## Trade and uneven development

- The development gap exists because some countries and regions have much greater **wealth, access to services, and life chances** than others
- Strategies are designed to reduce this gap — but each has **advantages and limitations**, depending on how it is applied
- **Trade **encourages LICs/MICs to sell goods on the global market to earn income

### Advantages

- It is often promoted as the key to long-term economic development
- It allows countries to sell its resources so they can invest in things to improve their development, such as education and healthcare
- This money means they can import goods which can further their development, such as tractors or communication technology

### Disadvantages

- Trading is not always fair
- Developing countries are usually paid less for their ***exports*** than developed countries
- Developing countries are disadvantaged by ***trade barriers***
- ***Trade agreements*** usually favour developed and emerging countries

### Fair Trade

- **Fair Trade** guarantees better prices and working conditions for producers
- It is an international movement that helps producers in poor countries get a fair deal by setting standards for trade

### Advantages

- Farming is done in an environmentally friendly way
- Product has a better position in the global market
- Part of the end price is invested back into the local community and future development projects
- **Example**: Over 90% of small coffee farmers in eastern Uganda have joined the **Gumutindo Coffee Cooperative**, which allows the coffee to be milled before roasting, which adds value to the coffee and increases the farmer's income

### Disadvantages

- **Fair Trade** products usually **cost more** than non-Fair Trade options, making them harder to buy and affecting sales
- Getting *certified* can be difficult and expensive for producers, especially for small farmers and those in remote areas
- Fair Trade can make producers dependent on it, which might be risky if demand changes
- The fair trade movement mainly focuses on a few products, like coffee and bananas, so options are limited for consumers

## International aid and uneven development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_64kkcZtpJ26Znt5Z` · Social, economic, and environmental strategies and techniques used to try to achieve sustainable development.

## International aid and uneven development

- Transfer of money, resources, or expertise from one country or organisation to another

  - Can be **emergency aid** (short-term) or **development aid** (long-term)
- Countries or **non-governmental organisations** (**NGO**s such as Oxfam) donate resources to a country to help or improve people’s lives
- Aid can take the form of money, emergency supplies, food, technology, specialist skills
- The aid helps** reduce the development gap** through **investing** in development projects

  - Focus is usually on health care, education and services
- Government-to-government aid (e.g. UK giving aid to rebuild roads or power plants in LICs) is a **top-down approach**
- **A bottom-up approach** is NGOs building schools, digging wells, or training midwives in rural communities

### Advantages

- Provides essential services (e.g. healthcare, education, clean water)
- Can **kick-start development** in poor regions
- Encourages goodwill and international cooperation

### Disadvantages

- Risk of **aid dependency** – countries rely on handouts instead of self-sufficiency
- Aid may be **tied** to conditions (e.g. must buy donor’s goods/services)
- Risk of **corruption or misuse** – money doesn’t always reach those who need it

## Debt relief and uneven development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_8tdzKXFPYJfBcFFb` · Social, economic, and environmental strategies and techniques used to try to achieve sustainable development.

## Debt relief and uneven development

- Not usually bottom-up, but **civil society campaigns** (e.g. Jubilee 2000) helped pressure governments to act
- Many developing and emerging countries owe money to other countries

  - Repayments and interest are expensive so they do not have money left to spend on development
  - Debt relief can mean that the debts are written off
- In 1996 the **Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC)** initiative was launched, which aimed to ensure that no country faces a debt burden it cannot manage
- In 2005, as part of the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),** the **Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI)** was added to supplement the HIPC and allowed for 100% debt relief on any money owed to the **IMF**, **World Bank** or **African Development Fund (AfDF)**
- The money saved can now be used for development projects such as industry, resources and infrastructure
- **Example**: Ugandan government has spent money to provide safe water to over 2 million people

### Advantages

- Cancels or reduces **international debts** owed by LICs
- Frees up money for **education, health, and infrastructure** instead of debt repayment
- Can create a **fresh start** for struggling economies

### Disadvantages

- Not all countries qualify for debt relief
- May come with conditions (e.g. cutting public spending or privatising services)
- Doesn’t fix the **underlying causes** of poverty or prevent future debt
- Corrupt governments may keep money

> **Exam Hint**
> In a 'To what extent' or 'Evaluate' question, always compare advantages and disadvantages, include both top-down and bottom-up examples, and reach a reasoned conclusion.

title: Strategies to achieve sustainable development
bodyMd:
# Strategies to achieve sustainable development

## Specification link

This page covers section 8.3.2 of the [CIE IGCSE specification](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/718150-2027-2029-syllabus.pdf) .

- **8.3.2 **- Social, economic and environmental strategies used to try and achieve sustainable development.

## Achieving sustainable development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_qf3nPv5C8N9qkbtH`

## Achieving sustainable development

- There is no single strategy that can close the **development gap **in a sustainable way
- There is often a dispute as to whether trade or aid is better for development
- These strategies can be categorised into  **social, economic and environmental sustainable development **and then classified into **top-down** or **bottom-up** approaches

> **Exam Hint**
> When evaluating a strategy, always ask, 'Who decided this? Who benefits most?'

## Social strategies to achieve sustainable development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_6qBfjyG9bwcYfWNp` · Social, economic, and environmental strategies and techniques used to try to achieve sustainable development

## Social strategies to achieve sustainable development

### Definition

- These strategies aim to improve **quality of life**, reduce **inequality**, and ensure access to **basic services** like education, healthcare, housing, and clean water

### Examples

- **Education programmes** (especially for girls and rural communities)

  - Improves literacy, job opportunities, and population control through informed family planning
- **Vaccination and healthcare initiatives**

  - Reduces disease spread and improves life expectancy
- **Informal settlement upgrading and social housing**

  - Provides safe, secure housing in urban areas without destroying communities
- **Access to clean water and sanitation**

  - Reduces waterborne diseases and improves hygiene

### Outcomes

- Long-term improvement in **human capital** and productivity
- Greater equality and **social stability**
- Informed citizens who can contribute to sustainable decision-making

### Challenges

- Requires **long-term investment** with slow results
- Can be **underfunded** in LICs
- Difficult to implement in conflict zones or areas of weak *governance*

## Economic strategies to achieve sustainable development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_F8jZCRz2NJZ979fh` · Social, economic, and environmental strategies and techniques used to try to achieve sustainable development

## Economic strategies to achieve sustainable development

### Definition

- These strategies focus on **creating jobs**, encouraging **fair and inclusive growth**, and reducing poverty without harming future prospects

### Examples

- **Microfinance and small business support**

  - Helps people (especially women) start local businesses, especially in LICs
- **Fair trade initiatives **

  - Ensures farmers and producers in LICs are paid fair prices
- **Sustainable agriculture and agroforestry **

  - Balances food production with environmental care
- **Green job creation** (e.g. solar technicians, sustainable transport workers)

  - Promotes employment in eco-friendly sectors

### Outcomes

- Reduces poverty and **income inequality**
- Builds a **resilient economy** not dependent on unsustainable industries
- Encourages **local development** and self-sufficiency

### Challenges

- May still rely on **external funding or aid**
- **Corruption or weak infrastructure** can reduce effectiveness
- Global market changes can impact vulnerable economies

## Environmental strategies to achieve sustainable development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_CBHgJmgyBjD5yvDr` · Social, economic, and environmental strategies and techniques used to try to achieve sustainable development

## Environmental strategies to achieve sustainable development

### Definition

- These strategies aim to **protect ecosystems**, reduce pollution and carbon emissions, and ensure natural resources are not overused or destroyed

### Examples

- **Renewable energy** (solar, wind, hydro)

  - Replaces fossil fuels and reduces greenhouse gas emissions
- **Forest conservation and afforestation**

  - Protects biodiversity and stores carbon
- **Sustainable fishing and farming **

  - Maintains natural stocks and soil fertility long-term
- **Waste reduction and recycling programmes **

  - Reduces landfill use and pollution

### Outcomes

- Slows down **climate change**
- Protects **ecosystem services** (e.g. pollination, clean water, fertile soil)
- Supports **eco-tourism** and green branding

### Challenges

- Often **expensive to implement** upfront
- Needs **global cooperation** (e.g. on climate agreements)
- Risk of **greenwashing** – companies claiming to be sustainable without real action

## Top-down vs bottom-up strategies

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_FfDg3M7tSMYt8Hvt`

## Top-down vs bottom-up strategies

| Type of Strategy | Definition | Who Leads? | Typical Characteristics |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Top-down** | Planned and implemented by **governments or international organisations**, often with **large-scale funding** | External agencies or national governments | Expensive, large-scale, may not meet local needs fully |
| **Bottom-up** | Initiated by **local people or communities**, often on a **small scale** | NGOs, grassroots groups, community leaders | Low-cost, locally appropriate, high community involvement |

- Top-down can be **effective** and **helpful**, but may **ignore local context**
- Bottom-up is **more inclusive** and **appropriate**, but may **lack funding or scalability**
- Best results often come from a **blend** of both: Government provides infrastructure, and communities manage and maintain it

### Top-down strategies

- These tend to be **government-led **or** donor-funded**, aiming for **widespread impact**:

  - **Vaccination and national healthcare programmes** are social strategy, often run by ministries of health or international bodies (e.g. WHO)
  - **National slum upgrading schemes **tend to be large-scale government-led improvements (e.g. sewage systems, housing infrastructure)
  - **Renewable energy projects like hydroelectric dams **are environmental strategies but are costly and often run by states or corporations
  - **Green job creation as part of national economic plans **are economic strategies that involve planning from national development offices or ministries
  - **Afforestation programmes led by national parks authorities **are environmental strategies and may involve land use laws and state-owned land

### Bottom-up strategies

- These are usually **community-led** and **locally driven**, addressing immediate local needs:

  - **Microfinance and small business support **are economic strategies that are often managed by NGOs or co-operatives empowering individuals (especially women)
  - **Fair trade schemes **is an economic strategy that supports small farmers and local producers with better market access
  - **Community-based education programmes **are social strategies where NGOs train local teachers or build schools with community help
  - **Recycling and local waste management initiatives **are environmental strategies led by community groups or NGOs in urban neighbourhoods
  - **Sustainable agriculture practices (e.g. composting, crop rotation)** fit into environmental and economic strategies and are usually adopted by small-scale farmers and local training groups

title: What is sustainable development?
bodyMd:
# What is sustainable development?

## Specification link

This page covers section 8.3.1 of the [CIE IGCSE specification](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/718150-2027-2029-syllabus.pdf) .

- **8.3.1 **- Definition(s) of sustainable development.

## Definitions of sustainable development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_yJdmPy9KYN5hDsjT` · Definitions of sustainable development

## Definitions of sustainable development

> **blockquote**
> Sustainable development aims to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own.
> (Brundtland Report, 1987)

- This involves:

  - Using resources **wisely** and **fairly**
  - Thinking about the **long-term impacts** of development
  - Balancing **economic growth**, **social well-being**, and **environmental protection**

### The three pillars of sustainability

- Sustainable development has **three interconnected areas**:

#### 1. Social sustainability

- Ensures people have access to basic needs like **healthcare, education, clean water, and housing**

  - Reduces inequality and improves **quality of life**
  - Builds **strong communities** and supports **cultural traditions**
- Example: Investing in education so future generations are skilled and empowered

#### 2. Economic sustainability

- Develops a country’s economy **without overusing resources**

  - Creates **jobs** and income that are long-lasting
  - Encourages **responsible business practices** and **fair trade**
- Example: Supporting local farmers instead of importing food from far away

  - Eco-tourism brings money into a country and supports local employment whilst protecting the environment

#### 3. Environmental sustainability

- Protects the planet’s **ecosystems**, **climate**, and **natural resources**

  - Reduces **pollution**, **waste**, and **carbon emissions**
  - Uses **renewable energy** (e.g. wind, solar) instead of fossil fuels
- Example: Using solar panels instead of burning coal for electricity

### Why is sustainable development important?

- The Earth has **limited resources** – if we use too much now, future generations may suffer
- **Climate change**, **deforestation**, **water shortages**, and **loss of biodiversity** are global problems caused by unsustainable practices
- Sustainable development helps achieve a **better quality of life for everyone**, now and in the future

> **Exam Hint**
> It is important to think geographically when discussing sustainability.  Think about suitable responses to the following questions to demonstrate to the examiner what it means to think like a geographer.
> 
> - Are we using more than we can replace?
> - Who benefits and who suffers from development choices?
> - What are the long-term effects of today’s actions?

> **Case Study**
> **Costa Rica – Eco-tourism and sustainable development**
> 
> **Location**
> 
> - **Costa Rica** is a small country in **Central America**, bordered by Nicaragua and Panama
> - It is famous for its **biodiverse rainforests, volcanoes, and coastlines**
> - Costa Rica has made **eco-tourism** (sustainable nature-based tourism) a central part of its development strategy
> 
> **Environmental sustainability**
> 
> - Over **25% of the land** is protected in **national parks and nature reserves**
> - Eco-lodges are built using **sustainable materials **and are often powered by **renewable energy** (like solar panels)
> - Visitors are encouraged to follow **‘leave no trace’** principles — no litter, no pollution, and respect wildlife
> - The result is that rainforests are preserved, and endangered species like the jaguar and sloth are protected
> 
> **Economic sustainability**
> 
> - Tourism is Costa Rica’s **largest foreign income source**
> - Eco-tourism brings money into **rural communities**
> - Local people work as **tour guides, lodge owners, craft sellers, and park rangers**
> - The result is that long-term jobs are created without destroying the environment
> 
> **Social sustainability**
> 
> - Education and training for locals in **wildlife conservation, hospitality, and English**
> - Improved local services such as **schools, water supply, and health clinics** funded by tourism revenue
> - Communities have a **voice in how tourism is managed**
> - This has resulted in a **higher quality of life** and a stronger **community resilience**
> 
> **Challenges**
> 
> - Some areas have become **over-dependent** on tourism
> - There is a need to balance **visitor numbers** with **ecosystem protection**
> - Income from tourism is uneven – popular areas earn more than remote regions
> 
> **Conclusion**
> 
> - Costa Rica shows how **sustainable tourism** can protect the environment, support local people, and grow the economy
> - It’s a leading example of how countries can **achieve sustainable development** by **valuing nature over exploitation**

title: Global pattern of development
bodyMd:
# Global pattern of development

## Specification link

This page covers section 8.2.2 of the [CIE IGCSE specification.](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/718150-2027-2029-syllabus.pdf)

**8.2.2 **- The current global pattern of low-income countries (LICs), middle-income countries (MICs) and high-income countries (HICs).

## Global pattern of development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_BtBjtBQDbyqgJp5W` · The current global pattern of low-income countries (LICs), middle-income countries (MICs) and high-income countries (HICs).

## Global pattern of development

- All countries move through different stages of development; they are not in fixed categories
- The UN identifies **four main stages of development**

![Chart showing stages of economic development over time: least developed, developing, newly industrialised, and developed countries.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/fc98dca97349-52628-stages-of-development-1.png)

*Graph showing the stages of development*

- Economic development is a **constantly shifting process** – countries can move up or down
- The **World Bank** regularly revises income classifications based on updated **GNI data**

  - For example: China moved from LIC to MIC in under 40 years due to** rapid industrialisation** and **trade integration**

### Low-income countries (LICs) and developing countries

- The countries with the lowest level of development are the **low-income countries (LICs) **(e.g., Chad, Nepal)
- Most people have a poor quality of life with inadequate services and few opportunities
- The UN reviews the list of LICs every three years

  - There are currently **44 LICs **(Dec. 2024)
  
    - Africa – 31 countries
    - Asia – 8 countries
    - Caribbean – 1 country
    - Small Island Developing States (SIDS) – 4 countries
- The criteria for inclusion on the list of LICs are:

  - **Gross National Income (GNI)** below US\$1,018
  - **Poor health** and **education levels**
  - **Economic and environmental vulnerability**
- The LICs and developing countries are:

  - at a disadvantage in world trade
  - vulnerable to natural hazards
  - lacking infrastructure
  - dependent on primary resources
- **Colonialism** has also impacted all 44 of the LICs and many **developing countries**, leading to:

  - depletion of resources
  - environmental degradation

### Middle-income countries (MICs)

- **Middle-income countries (MICs) **are also known as** newly industrialised countries (NICs)**

  - These countries are experiencing rapid economic growth and development based on industrial development
  - Incomes are rising and most people enjoy a reasonable standard of living
  - Countries that have become MICs include:
  
    - Singapore
    - South Korea
    - Brazil
    - China
    - India

### High-income countries (HICs)

- These countries have **modern industries** and people enjoy a** good standard of living **with **relatively high levels of income**
- Good level of services
- Countries that have become HICs include:

  - Norway
  - Saudi Arabia
  - Japan
  - Uruguay
  - Canada
- The global pattern of distribution is complicated and changes constantly
- However, there are some key features

  - Asia and Africa have more MICs than LICs
  - Most HICs and MICs are found in the northern hemisphere
  - LICs are mostly in the southern hemisphere
  - Eastern European countries have been classified as MICs
  - Most South American countries are MICs

![World map showing income levels by country: dark green for high income, light green for upper-middle, light purple for lower-middle, dark purple for low.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/82493bf3a0a9-4155-stages-of-development.png)

*Distribution of global development*

### Why classifications are contested or dynamic

- **GNI per capita doesn’t tell the full story** – it hides regional inequalities (e.g. urban vs. rural divide)
- A country may be **wealthy overall but still have large impoverished populations**
- **Data reliability** can vary – weak governance or poor census systems affect accuracy
- **Political sensitivity** – calling a country an LIC can change how people see it and affect its chances for aid
- **Development is multi-dimensional –** just because a place is rich doesn’t mean people are happy or the environment is strong

> **Exam Hint**
> Classifications can change, but issues like inequality, corruption, and environmental risks might remain.

title: Levels of development
bodyMd:
# Levels of development

## Specification link

This page covers section 8.2.1 of the [CIE IGCSE specification](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/718150-2027-2029-syllabus.pdf) .

- **8.2.1 **- Reasons for differences in levels of development and the development gap, to include social, economic, and environmental factors.

## What is the development gap?

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_3TwjsNMYhkM24Cvp` · Reasons for differences in levels of development and the development gap, to include social, economic, and environmental factors. 

## What is the development gap?

- The **development gap **is the difference in levels of development between the least developed and most developed countries in the world
- The development gap shows how different these countries are in terms of their wealth, health, and general quality of life
- The development gap affects how well millions of people live, with high-income countries usually having better living standards and more resources
- The development gap can cause problems like

  - poverty
  - inequality
  - harm to the environment
  - social unrest
- The development gap affects global stability and security because problems in poorer countries can impact the wider world

## Reasons for the differences in development

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_V7r24HWNzs6Bj7JZ` · Reasons for differences in levels of development and the development gap, to include social, economic, and environmental factors. 

## Reasons for the differences in development

- The development gap is a complex problem with many **social, economic and environmental reasons**
- These reasons can become less or more important over time

![Diagram illustrating factors affecting development and human welfare: food and water security, economic, government, resources, social, cultural, technological.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/2153b78b7192-8218-factors-affecting-development-and-human-wel.png)

*Factors affecting development and human welfare*

## Environmental factors

- ***Landlocked*** countries have no direct access to ports, making **trade **more difficult and they often **develop more slowly **as a result

  - Nine of the twelve most undeveloped countries in the world are landlocked and struggle to trade with other countries
- Countries with **extreme climates** develop more slowly, as climate impacts agricultural productivity and infrastructure
- **Natural disasters** such as earthquakes and floods occur more frequently in some countries, which diverts money from development to recovery
- **Climate-related diseases and pests,** such as **malaria**, affect the ability of the population to stay healthy enough to work

  - **Locust swarms** can decimate crops

- Some countries can meet all their needs from the **natural resources** they have
- Many countries have to ***import*** some natural resources that are not available within their borders
- **Water, food** and **energy security** are vital to support a country's development

## Social factors

- *Demography*

  - The **birth** and **death rates**, as well as **immigration,** affect the available workforce
  - Some countries have a large, youthful population but lack education and employment opportunities
- **Technology**

  - Can help to increase water, food and energy security
  - **Mechanisation** of farming increases yields and improved land surveying may reveal more energy sources
- **Conflict and instability** can disrupt economic development, hinder investment, and displace populations
- **Levels of education** affect the skills people have. The more educated a population is, the more a country will develop
- **Healthcare** affects how well people are, which affects their ability to work
- **Lack of equality** can mean that the overall productivity of a country is affected
- **Colonialism – **Some countries' **colonial past** has caused uneven growth, environmental degradation, loss of cultural systems and inequality

  - Colonial powers, such as the UK, France, and Spain, extracted resources from colonies, such as minerals and crops, leaving little wealth behind
  - They also set up systems that benefited themselves, not local people
  - This caused inequality and left many countries dependent on low-value exports after independence
  - Many African and American countries were impacted due to the transatlantic slave trade

## Economic factors

- **Corruption **can take money away from important projects and make it hard to put good policies into action
- LICs usually **trade **primary products for less money to HICs

  - The HIC then produces a final, **high-profit **product
- HICs have good road, railway, and electricity **infrastructure**

  - This helps attract foreign investment because companies can quickly produce and transport goods
  - This boosts a country's development by bringing in money

> **Exam Hint**
> **Think systemically** about the causes of the development gap. How do social, economic, and environmental factors interlink to either widen or close the development gap?
> 
> For example: low investment in education → low literacy → limited skilled workforce → low-income economy → poor healthcare → high infant mortality
> 
> Identify **feedback loops **or **spirals—**both **positive **and **negative**—to understand how development shifts or combines over time.   For example, economic inequality leads to social unrest, which in turn damages the environment.

title: How to Answer 5 Mark Decision-Making Questions
bodyMd:
# How to Answer 5 Mark Decision-Making Questions

## What is a decision-making question?

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_NbwhGhmsbCT4kt4B`

## What is a decision-making question?

- The 5-mark questions in **Paper 1 **and **Paper 2 **are **Section B, Question 3 b(ii)**
- The questions give you **information about different options and ask you to choose between them**
- This tests a specific AO3 skill: *"make and justify a decision based upon information provided."*

### Command phrases and assessment objectives

- This question uses the command phrase "**justify your decision**"

  - The question tests:
  
    - **AO3 (Evaluation and decision-making)**

### How this question is marked

- Unlike the longer 7-mark decision making question, these are **point-marked, not levels-marked**

  - You are awarded marks for specific content points, with **one mark specifically reserved for your evaluation or judgement**
  - You're reading resources rather than recalling your own knowledge, and you must **commit to one option**, not just weigh up pros and cons in the abstract

## How marks are awarded 

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_XpDSQTmz6bfHssGZ`

## How marks are awarded

- Up to **4 marks** for relevant points

  - Either four simple points, or fewer points developed further (a point plus its development counts as 2 marks)
- **1 mark** is reserved specifically for a stated evaluation or judgement

  - This means you cannot get full marks from a list of facts alone, however accurate
  - **The judgement mark only comes from an evaluative statement**

### Structuring your answer

- Give three to four relevant points (advantages of the plan you have selected and disadvantages of the plans you have rejected), briefly developed rather than just named
- Finish your answer with a clear evaluative sentence

  - A word like **"however"**, **"overall"** or **"ultimately"** is often the signal that you have reached your judgement

### Assessment objectives

- These 5 mark questions are used to assess **AO3: Evaluation and decision-making**
- This means you are expected to**:**

  - Evaluating the importance of geographical factors, processes and change
  - Recognise the limitations of data, theories and models
  - Evaluate the impact of different values and attitudes in environmental management; making and justifying decisions
  - Weigh up the options available to decision-makers
  - Evaluating the success of management strategies, including sustainable approaches

> **Worked Example**
> Study Table 3.1, which shows three plans which the government of a country in Africa is considering to sustainably manage the tropical rainforest.
> 
> ![Table 3.1 details plans for rainforest development: Plan A involves restricted areas and replanting; Plan B focuses on conservation; Plan C supports ecotourism.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/426e56fea29c-17345-screenshot-2025-07-02-135000.png)
> 
> Choose the plan that you think will be the most effective in sustainably managing the tropical rainforest. Justify your decision.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> Plan chosen -  A
> 
> Justification  - Plan A has several advantages by restricting the places where development can happen it will prevent large scale destruction** [1]** and the development can be focussed on areas which do not contain sensitive ecosystems** [d]**. The planting of trees also means that more trees will be planted than removed** [1]**. However, there are disadvantages such as the new trees planted will take time to grow **[1]** but the advantages of this plan outweigh the disadvantages **[1]**.
> 
> The command word is 'justify' this means the answer needs to include valid reasons to support the point of view given. The answer must explain why it is the best option.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for evaluation/judgement** [1]**
> - 1 mark for each simple point **[1] **
> - 1 mark for each developed point **[d]**
> 
> Answers can be either:
> 
> - 4 simple points plus evaluation
> - 1 developed point plus 2 simple points plus evaluation
> - 2 points which are developed plus evaluation
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Common errors where students lose marks include:
> 
>   - Not including judgement or evaluation within the answer
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - **Plan B **
> 
>   - The area will be conserved
>   - Ecosystems will not be destroyed
>   - Resources will not be exploited
>   - May affect the growth of the economy
> - **Plan C**
> 
>   - Development can be controlled
>   - The community can be involved in decision making/jobs
>   - Many areas have already been destroyed

title: How to Answer 7 Mark Decision-Making Questions
bodyMd:
# How to Answer 7 Mark Decision-Making Questions

## What is a decision-making question?

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_qkN8rqnXkbNh9TZ5`

## What is a decision-making question?

- The 7-mark decision making question in **Paper 2 Section A** doesn't ask you to evaluate a general statement

  - The question gives you **evidence about two named options and asks you to choose between them**
  - This tests a specific AO3 skill: *"make and justify a decision based upon information provided."*
- Like the "assess the extent to which" question, this is marked using **levels of response **but the task itself is different

  - You're reading resources (a map extract, photographs, graphs) rather than recalling your own knowledge, and you must **commit to one option**, not just weigh up pros and cons in the abstract

### Command phrases and assessment objectives

- This question uses the command phrase "**justify your decision**"

  - The question tests:
  
    - **AO1 (Knowledge and understanding) **
    - **AO3 (Evaluation and decision-making)**

### How the question is marked

- Unlike the 5-mark "Evaluate" questions elsewhere on the paper, this question is **not point-marked**
- The examiner reads your whole answer and decides which level it best fits, then places it within that level's mark range
- Within a level examiners award:

  - The top mark if your answer **convincingly** meets the level statement
  - The middle mark if it **adequately** meets it
  - The bottom mark if it **just** meets it

#### Level 3 (6-7 marks)

- A balanced/comprehensive answer which shows a clear understanding with developed statements which are relevant to the question
- Answer is supported by relevant evidence and/or examples throughout
- Answer contains a supported evaluation/judgement/decision on the question

#### Level 2 (3-5 marks)

- An answer which shows a good understanding with developed statements which are relevant to the question
- Answer is supported by some relevant evidence and/or examples
- Answer contains a limited evaluation/judgement/decision on the question

#### Level 1 (1-2 marks)

- An answer which shows limited understanding using simple statements which are relevant to the question

#### Level 0 (0 marks)

- No creditable response

## How to structure your answer

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_YcJvYq82sykn2s7h`

## How to structure your answer

- **State your chosen option clearly and immediately**

  - Don't leave the examiner to infer your decision from the body of your answer
- **Use evidence from every resource you're given**, not just one

  - If you're told to refer to a map extract and two photographs
  - A Level 3 answer draws on all of them, not just the easiest one
- **Compare, don't just describe**

  - For each point, say what it means for *both* locations, not just why your chosen one is good
- **Reach a final justified decision**

  - This is your judgement, so make sure your closing point directly answers "which is most suitable," not just "here are some facts about each"

### How to answer a 7 mark decision-making question?

#### Step 1

- Read the question carefully and underline the **command words**

*"*Use evidence from the map extract and Figures 1.2 and 1.3 to identify which location you consider to be the most suitable for the TNC to locate the factory.

Refer to Location **A** and **B **when <u>justifying your decision</u>."

- The command word "**justify**" means that you need to support a case with evidence/argument

#### Step 2

- Underline the key words.

*"*<u>Use evidence</u> from the map extract and Figures 1.2 and 1.3 to <u>identify which location</u> you consider to be the <u>most suitable for the TNC to locate the factory</u>.

Refer to Location **A** and **B **when justifying your decision."

- In this example, you need to make a decision about which is the most suitable location for the factory and why.

#### Step 3

- Plan the information you are going to include. This can be a short list of bullet points. For example:

  - Flat land
  - Transport links and accessibility
  - Proximity to workers
  - Infrastructure

#### Step 4

- Write your answer

  - To achieve 7 marks, you need to write at least 3 detailed statements
  - Do not make general statements
  - Be specific, for example:

> **Worked Example**
> A TNC is considering the following locations for its factory.
> 
> Location **A:  **At Newport West, in and around grid square 6748. Figure 1.2  is a photograph of this area.
> 
> Location **B: **At Bridgeport, in and around grid square 6244. Figure 1.3  is a photograph of this area.
> 
> [Map extract](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/719016-2027-specimen-paper-survey-map-2.pdf)
> 
> ![Top image: Newport West port with cranes and cargo ship on a sunny day. Bottom image: Aerial view of Bridgeport with buildings and mountains in the background.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/be5237ed0634-43712-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads20250746055.png)
> 
> Use evidence from the map extract and Figures 1.2 and 1.3 to identify which location you consider to be the most suitable for the TNC to locate the factory.
> 
> Refer to Location **A** and **B **when justifying your decision.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> Location chosen:  B,  Bridgeport.
> 
> Location B is more suitable for a TNC to build its factory. **[E] **It has flat land, **[KU] **which will make construction easier and cheaper. **[E]** The land also appears cleared, **[KU] **reducing the cost of preparation. **[E] **There is a main road running through grid square 6244 **[KU], **allowing the easy transport of goods and workers. **[E]** A railway line also passes nearby, **[KU] **which is important for importing raw materials or exporting products. **[E]**
> 
> Location A is less ideal because it's on hilly land **[KU]**,** **making construction harder and more expensive. **[E] **The area also has more vegetation, **[KU] **which means that clearing land would take more time and money. **[E] **Although there is some road access **[KU]**,** **it is not as direct or developed as in Location B. **[E]**
> 
> Furthermore, Location B is closer to Bridgeport **[KU]**, a town that would provide more work, housing, and services for employees. **[E]** The map shows nearby built-up areas **[KU]**, which could help access skilled labour and essential infrastructure, such as power and water supplies. **[E]** Location A is further from towns and more isolated. **[KU]**
> 
> In conclusion, Location B has flatter land, better transport links and is nearer to urban services, making it the most suitable option for a TNC factory. **[E]**
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This is a level of response answer. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark. Marks are allocated against two assessment objectives:
> 
> - **AO1 Knowledge and Understanding** **[KU]**
> - **AO3**** ****Evaluation and decision making**** [E]**
> 
> A top-level 3** [7 mark] **answer will have a balanced, developed and evidenced answer that demonstrates knowledge and understanding **[KU]** to evaluate (judge or decide) **[E]** where a TNC may locate its factory.

> **Exam Hint**
> Always name your chosen location in your very first sentence, and use "Location A"/"Location B" (or the place names) throughout — don't switch to vague terms like "the first one."
> 
> Marks are for using the evidence you're given, so if you're referred to a map extract as well as photographs, make sure your answer draws on both. An answer that only discusses the photos and ignores the map, when the map was named in the question, will not reach Level 3 even if the writing is otherwise strong.

title: How to Answer a 5 mark \"Evaluate\" Question
bodyMd:
# How to Answer a 5 mark "Evaluate" Question

## How to answer 5-Mark "Evaluate" questions

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_7bbFDxX72qMWq6ts`

## How to answer 5-Mark questions

- In CIE IGCSE Geography (0460), **"Evaluate"**, **"To what extent" or "Assess the extent" **questions appear as the **(b)(ii)** part of **Section B** (Questions 2 and 4)

  - They are found in both Paper 1 and Paper 2 and are worth **5 marks**
- Unlike the longer 7-mark questions on this paper, these are **point-marked, not levels-marked**

  - There is no best-fit judgement made by the examiner
  - You are awarded marks for specific content points, with **one mark specifically reserved for your evaluation or judgement**

### How the marks are awarded

- Up to **4 marks** for relevant points

  - Either four simple points, or fewer points which are developed further (a point plus its development counts as 2 marks)
- **1 mark** is reserved specifically for a stated evaluation or judgement

  - This means you cannot get full marks from a list of facts alone, however accurate they are
  - **The judgement mark only comes from an evaluative statement**

### Structuring your answer

- Give three to four relevant points (strategies, factors, or ideas), briefly developed rather than just named
- Finish your answer with a clear evaluative sentence

  - A word like **"however"**, **"overall"** or **"ultimately"** is often the signal that you have reached your judgement
- Common judgement you may need to make for management/strategy questions include:

  - Which option works best and why
  - What determines success (e.g. level of economic development, available technology or finance),
  - A limitation shared by all the strategies

### Assessment objectives

- These 5 mark questions are used to assess **AO3: Evaluation and decision-making**
- This means you are expected to**:**

  - Evaluating the importance of geographical factors, processes and change
  - Recognise the limitations of data, theories and models
  - Evaluate the impact of different values and attitudes in environmental management; making and justifying decisions
  - Weigh up the options available to decision-makers
  - Evaluating the success of management strategies, including sustainable approaches

> **Worked Example**
> **Evaluate the different ways in which the impacts of tropical storms (cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons) can be managed.**
> 
> [5]
> 
> **Answer using four simple points and a final evaluation/judgement**
> 
> Shelters for people to take refuge in during a storm **[1]** Warning systems (e.g. satellite tracking) to alert people in advance **[1] **Evacuation planning — moving people away from high-risk areas before landfall **[1]** Storm defences built to protect coastal areas. **[1] **However, storms cannot be prevented, only managed. The success of strategies often depends on a country's wealth, as HICs can afford better warning systems and defences than LICs. **[1]**
> 
> **An alternative answer with development of two points rather than four simple points**
> 
> Shelters for people to take refuge in during a storm** [1] t**hese are effective at managing the impacts because they are built to withstand the strong winds and high rainfall**. [d]  **Warning systems (e.g satellite tracking) to alert people ahead of the storm **[1] **which means that they can evacuate to safety or prepare their homes to reduce the impact.** [d] **However, storms cannot be prevented, only managed. The success of strategies often depends on a country's wealth, as HICs can afford better warning systems and defences than LICs. **[1]**
> 
> **Mark Scheme and Guidance**
> 
> - 4 marks for any four relevant strategies, one mark each
> 
> - 1 mark is reserved specifically for evaluation or judgement
> 
> - Fewer, more developed points also work: a point plus its development can earn 2 marks, in any combination that reaches the 4-mark cap for content

> **Exam Hint**
> Do not spend all five minutes listing strategies — the fourth mark for content is easy to reach, but many students lose the fifth mark entirely by never writing a judgement. Build in your evaluation from the start: as you name each strategy, keep asking yourself "but does this actually work, and for whom?" One clear evaluative sentence at the end is enough to secure that mark.

title: How to Answer an \"Assess the extent to which\" 7 Mark Question
bodyMd:
# How to Answer an "Assess the extent to which" 7 Mark Question

## What is an "Assess the extent to which.." question?

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_TRzhWBJrZvNChGvM`

## What is an "Assess the extent to which.." question?

- In CIE IGCSE Geography (0460), there are two types of 7 mark question

  - In** Section A** on each of Paper 1 and 2 there is a 7 mark "**Assess the extent to which**" question which requires an** evaluative judgement **
  - In** Section B **(Questions 2–4(c)), the 7 mark questions use "**Explain**" or "**Describe**" and only test knowledge
  
    - No judgement is required there

### Command phrase and assessment objectives

- This question uses command phrases like **"Assess the extent to which..."**

  - The question tests:
  
    - **AO1 (Knowledge and understanding) **
    - **AO3 (Evaluation and decision-making)**

### How the question is marked

- Unlike the 5-mark "Evaluate" questions elsewhere on the paper, this question is **not point-marked**
- The examiner reads your whole answer and decides which level it best fits, then places it within that level's mark range
- Within a level examiners award:

  - The top mark if your answer **convincingly** meets the level statement
  - The middle mark if it **adequately** meets it
  - The bottom mark if it **just** meets it

#### Level 3 (6-7 marks)

- A balanced/comprehensive answer which shows a clear understanding with developed statements which are relevant to the question
- Answer is supported by relevant evidence and/or examples throughout
- Answer contains a supported evaluation/judgement/decision on the question

#### Level 2 (3-5 marks)

- An answer which shows a good understanding with developed statements which are relevant to the question
- Answer is supported by some relevant evidence and/or examples
- Answer contains a limited evaluation/judgement/decision on the question

#### Level 1 (1-2 marks)

- An answer which shows limited understanding using simple statements which are relevant to the question

#### Level 0 (0 marks)

- No creditable response

### What separates Level 2 from Level 3?

- **Level 2** answers tend to describe points on both sides of the argument, but without much supporting detail, and the judgement is only implied or very brief
- **Level 3** answers name specific, developed evidence or examples for each point. It  outlines not just that "technology can help" but exactly how. It ends with a clear, supported judgement that directly answers "to what extent"

## How to answer an "Assess the extent to which.." question

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_kJDbdsDS7gxfPChH`

## How to answer an "Assess the extent to which.." question

### Step 1

- Read the question carefully and underline the **command words**

*"*<u>*Assess the extent to which*</u>*technology can reduce the impacts of volcanic eruptions*."

- The command word "**Assess**" means that at the end of your answer you need to make an informed judgement

### Step 2

- Underline the key words.

*"Assess the extent to which* <u>*technology* </u>*can* <u>*reduce the impacts*</u>*of volcanic* <u>*eruptions*</u>."

- In this example, you need to focus on examples of technology which can reduce the impacts of volcanic eruptions

### Step 3

- Plan the information you are going to include. This can be a short list of bullet points. For example:

  - Brief definition of outline of some technologies
  - How the technologies work and their effectiveness
  - Limitations of technologies
  - Final judgement about whether technology can reduce the impacts of eruptions

### Step 4

- Write your answer

  - To achieve 7 marks, you need to write at least 3 detailed statements
  - Do not make general statements
  - Be specific, for example:

*'In Iceland, the eruption of Eyjafjallajökull in 2010 was predicted using seismic data, helping to reduce the impact on people.'*

- Whilst the question does not ask for a named volcano part of the criteria for level 3 is that the  '**Answer is supported by relevant evidence and/or examples throughout**'

> **Worked Example**
> **Assess the extent to which technology can reduce the impacts of volcanic eruptions.**
> 
> [7 marks]
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> Technology can significantly reduce the impacts of volcanic eruptions in several ways. Firstly, scientists can monitor seismic activity and volcanic gases to predict when a volcano might erupt. This allows early warnings to be issued and gives people time to evacuate safely **[KU]**. In Iceland, the eruption of Eyjafjallajökull in 2010 was predicted using seismic data, helping to reduce the impact on people **[KU]**.
> 
> Technology also helps during the eruption. Satellites and radar can track ash clouds so that planes can avoid them or airports can be closed, preventing dangerous incidents in the air **[KU]**. For example, the closure of Bali's international airport during the eruption of Mount Lewotobi Laki-Laki** [KU]**.
> 
> However, technology does have its limits. It cannot stop an eruption or control how powerful it is. Toxic gases and ash cannot be easily diverted, which still pose serious health risks and can cause long-term damage **[E]**. Not all countries can afford expensive monitoring equipment, meaning poorer areas may suffer more damage because of lack of early warning** [E]**.
> 
> In conclusion, while technology cannot prevent volcanic eruptions, it can play a major role in reducing their impacts, especially by giving people time to prepare. However, its effectiveness depends on the availability of resources and the type of eruption** [E].**
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This is a level of response answer. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark. Marks are allocated against two assessment objectives:
> 
> - **AO1 Knowledge and Understanding** **[KU]**
> - **AO3**** ****Evaluation and decision making**** [E]**
> 
> A top level 3 (7 mark) answer will have a balanced, developed and evidenced answer that demonstrates knowledge and understanding** [KU]** to evaluate (judge or decide) **[E]** how technology can reduce the impacts of volcanic eruption
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors where students lose marks:
> 
> - A lack of evaluation or judgement about the value of different technology types
> - A lack of evidence or examples to support the answer
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - Technology can be used to divert/slow down lava flows
> - Technology relating to improved transport and medical care
> - The magnitude of the eruption cannot be controlled

> **Exam Hint**
> Notice this answer names real technologies (seismometers, monitoring of gases, satellite monitoring) and real eruptions (Mount Lewotobi Laki-Laki and Eyjafjallajökull 2010) rather than just saying "technology helps" — that's what moves an answer from Level 2 ("some relevant evidence") into Level 3 ("supported by relevant evidence and/or examples throughout").
> 
> You don't need a full named case study here, since the question doesn't ask for one, but a few specific, real details do far more for your mark than extra generic sentences would.

title: How to use Detailed Specific Examples in 7 Mark Questions
bodyMd:
# How to use Detailed Specific Examples in 7 Mark Questions

## What is a detailed specific example?

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_2NpRHTCfWhgm8SF7`

## What is a detailed specific example?

- A **Detailed Specific Example (DSE)** is a real, named **case study** you use to answer certain questions on Paper 1 and Paper 2

  - This is a specific river, country, city, volcano or company, rather than a general description
- The syllabus does **not** name these examples for you: your teacher chooses which ones you study

  - You need to be able to name them precisely and use real detail from them in the exam

### Where are detailed specific examples required?

- There are **16 parts of the specification** across the ten topics that require a detailed specific example

  - Eight on Paper 1 (Physical Geography)
  - Eight on Paper 2 (Human Geography)

#### Paper 1

- **Changing river environments**

  - The causes, impacts and management of a flood for a named river
  - The causes, impacts and management of pollution in a named river

- **Changing coastal environments**

  - Coastal erosion and storm protection for a named country or coastal area
  - The importance, threats to, and protection of a named coral reef

- **Changing ecosystems**

  - Deforestation impacts and management for a named country or tropical rainforest area
- **Tectonic hazards**

  - The causes, impacts, responses and management of an earthquake for a named country or area
  - The causes, impacts, responses and management of an eruption for a named volcano

- **Climate change**

  - The impacts, responses and management of climate change for a named country or region

#### Paper 2

- **Changing populations **

  - The reasons for growth/decline and impacts of a population policy for a named country
  - The push and pull factors of a named international migration (named origin and destination country)
- **Changing towns and cities **

  - The opportunities, challenges and management of rapid urban growth for a named urban area
- **Development**

  - The level and strategies to raise development for a named MIC or LIC
- **Changing economies**

  - The impacts of globalisation and of a named TNC in a named country or area
  - The growth, benefits, problems and management of tourism in a named country or area
- **Resource provision**

  - The factors, problems and strategies around food supply in a named country or area
  - The energy mix, impacts and management of energy supply for a named country
- **The Antarctic ecosystem** is the one exception

  - The syllabus specifically does not require a DSE here, since the whole sub-topic is already based on Antarctica itself

## What is an 'explain' or 'describe' 7 mark question?

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_HGBHf7j3cxbP7CT5`

## What is an 'explain' or 'describe' 7 mark question?

- In CIE IGCSE Geography (0460), there are two types of 7 mark question

  - In** Section A** on each of Paper 1 and 2 there is a 7 mark "Assess the extent to which" question which requires an** evaluative judgement **
  - In** Section B **(Questions 2–4(c)), the 7 mark questions use "**Explain**" or "**Describe**" and only test knowledge
  
    - No judgement is required in these questions
- This guide will explain how to complete the **Section B** 7 mark questions

### Command phrases and assessment objectives

- This question type uses command phrases '**explain**' and '**describe**'
- The question tests:

  - **AO1 (Knowledge and understanding) **

### How are these questions marked?

- This question is **not point-marked,** it is a** levelled response **
- The examiner reads your whole answer and decides which level it best fits, then places it within that level's mark range
- Within a level examiners award:

  - The top mark if your answer **convincingly** meets the level statement
  - The middle mark if it **adequately** meets it
  - The bottom mark if it **just** meets it

#### Level 3 (6-7 marks)

- Uses named example (when appropriate)
- A comprehensive answer with developed statements showing detailed knowledge and understanding which is relevant to the question
- Answer includes specific details about place or process

#### Level 2 (3-5 marks)

- Developed statements showing good knowledge and understanding which is relevant to the question

#### Level 1 (1-2 marks)

- Simple statements with limited detail, showing basic knowledge and understanding which is relevant to the question

#### Level 0 (0 marks)

- No creditable response

## How to use a detailed specific example well

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_ZwMv5bcX3gMG5b9f`

## How to use a detailed specific example well

- **Name it precisely**

  - A real place, not a vague description
  - "Bangladesh" and "the River Ganges/Brahmaputra" score higher than "a poor country" or "a river in Asia"
- **Use specific facts**

  - Figures, dates, place names within the example
  - The mark schemes for these questions specifically reward "specific details about place or process," not general statements that could apply to anywhere

- **Match the example to the question**

  - Know what your named example is meant to illustrate (e.g. is it your flood example, or your pollution example, for that same river?) so you don't just use whichever example you remember best
- Examples from the **2000s onwards** tend to work best, since more recent data and reporting is usually available to draw on

### How to answer an 'in an area you have studied' question

#### Step 1

- Read the question carefully and underline the **command words**

*"*<u>**Explain**</u>** the importance of coral reefs to a coastal area you have studied.**"

- The command word "**explain**" means that you need to say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence

#### Step 2

- Underline the key words.

*"***Explain the **<u>**importance**</u>** of **<u>**coral reefs **</u>**to a coastal **<u>**area you have studied**</u>**.**"

- In this example, you need to focus on why coral reefs are important using your detailed specific example

#### Step 3

- Plan the information you are going to include. This can be a short list of bullet points. For example:

  - Where the coral reef is located
  - Reasons that it is important including:
  
    - Storm protection
    - Ecosystem
    - Reducing erosion
    - Tourism
    - Cultural significance

#### Step 4

- Write your answer

  - To achieve 7 marks, you need to write at least 3 detailed statements
  - Do not make general statements
  - Be specific, for example:

*'*the reef supports tourism by attracting millions of visitors for diving and snorkelling, which contributes over AU\$6 billion (about US\$4 billion) to the Australian economy each year.'*     *

> **Worked Example**
> **Explain the importance of coral reefs to a coastal area you have studied.**
> 
> [7 marks]
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> The Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of northeast Australia, is important for many reasons. Located off the coast of Queensland, Australia, it is the largest coral reef system in the world. **[KU] **The reef system acts as natural walls that absorb wave energy, protecting coastal towns from erosion and storm damage. **[KU]**
> 
> The reef is home to around 9,000 known marine species, so it helps biodiversity. **[KU] **This is important for the fishing industry, as many fish breed and live in the reef, providing jobs and food for local communities. **[KU]**
> 
> The reef has cultural significance, as Indigenous Australian groups like the Yirrganydji and Gurang people **[KU]** have cared for it for thousands of years using their traditional ecological knowledge. **[KU]** The reef's diversity has helped scientists to find medicines to treat diseases like cancer and arthritis. **[KU]**
> 
> In addition, the reef supports tourism by attracting millions of visitors for diving and snorkelling, **[KU]** which contributes over AU\$6 billion (about US\$4 billion) to the Australian economy each year. **[KU]** The reef, through tourism, recreation, and fishing, supports over 64,000 jobs. **[KU]**
> 
> Without the reef, Australia's coast would have less protection, which could potentially result in the loss of many jobs. **[KU]**
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This is a level of response answer. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark. Marks are allocated against one assessment objective:
> 
> - **AO1 Knowledge and Understanding** **[KU]**
> 
> This is a **'level of response'** answer. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> - A Level 3 answer will use specific examples that demonstrate detailed, developed knowledge and understanding **[KU]** of the importance of coral reefs in a specified coastal area.
> 
> **Alternative** **content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - The coast receives protection from tsunamis.
> - Provides sheltered anchorage and harbours.
> - It maintains marine ecosystems and food chains.

> **Exam Hint**
> Notice this question doesn't use "evaluate" or "assess" — it says "explain," so there's no judgement mark here, and the mark scheme (Table B) rewards knowledge and specific detail, not a balanced argument.
> 
> The biggest difference between a Level 2 and a Level 3 answer is specificity: naming "the Great Barrier Reef" and describing an actual named benefit scores far better than writing generically about "a coral reef." Build a bank of 3–4 real facts for each of your detailed specific examples well before the exam, rather than trying to recall detail under pressure.

title: Cartographic skills
bodyMd:
# Cartographic skills

## Maps

- Questions in the exam will be based on topographical maps

  - The maps can be from anywhere in the world
  - Maps will have a key, scale, northings and eastings
  - These all need to be used to answer the questions

## Grid references

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_m3CTDmjBhDWjWSKq` · Candidates should be able to: 
• select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols, a key, and other information 
• extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information presented on maps 
• use co-ordinates, latitude and longitude, 4 and 6 figure grid references 
• give directions using the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north 
• measure and estimate distances and area 
• use and interpret gradient, contour lines and spot heights; calculate differences in height 
• interpret cross-sections and transects.

## Grid references

### Grid references

- 4-figure are used to locate specific grid squares within the map

  - The first two figures are the **eastings**, which indicate how far east or west a grid is across the map
  - The second two figures are the **northings**, which indicate how far north or south a grid is on the map
- 6-figure grid references are used to locate exact points within grid squares

  - The first three figures are the eastings
  - The second three figures are the northings
- To find a 4- and 6 figure grid reference

  - To find the four-figure grid reference, give the number from the bottom of the map first, then the number from the side

![Grid with four squares, top-right shaded red. Black coordinates (17, 51) in red area. Red lines highlight square edges. Axes range 16-18, 50-52.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/6152e9feb457-4-figure-grid-reference.png)

*4 - figure grid reference*

- In image above, the 4-figure grid reference would be 17, 51
- To give the 6-figure grid reference, you need to imagine that the grid square is divided into 100 smaller squares

![Grid coordinates with red lines and arrow pointing to a pink square, labelled 175,512. Black grid overlay covers the top right quadrant.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/b898281e011c-4-figure-grid-reference-2.png)

*Six figure grid reference*

> **Worked Example**
> Figure 1.1 shows some of the features around the main settlement at Misterbianco in the north-east of the map extract
> 
> ![Map grid showing areas labelled A, B, C, D, E with a curved line crossing through. The name Misterbianco is marked near the centre.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/a466f430e00d-screenshot-2022-10-26-at-11-15-46.png)
> 
> What is the six-figure grid reference for the junction to the north of B in Fig. 1?
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Final answer:** **Answer**
> 
> - **017 517**

## Scale

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_VwcHz89r5f6Rpbn9` · Candidates should be able to: 
• select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols, a key, and other information 
• extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information presented on maps 
• use co-ordinates, latitude and longitude, 4 and 6 figure grid references 
• give directions using the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north 
• measure and estimate distances and area 
• use and interpret gradient, contour lines and spot heights; calculate differences in height 
• interpret cross-sections and transects.

## Scale

- Maps in exams will be scaled at either:

  - 1:25,000 (1 cm = 250 m in real life)
  - 1:50,000 (1 cm = 500 m in real life)
- Distance measurement methods:

  - For straight or nearly straight distances:
  
    - Use a ruler
    - Use the edge of a straight piece of paper
  - Using map scale:
  
    - Mark distances on a piece of paper using the scale at the map's bottom
    - Lay the marked paper from first to second point to calculate distance

![Topographic map section with contour lines, elevation gradients, and roads marked N86. Features locations like Fme de Missoule and L'her de Lembree.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/7339e5dca40f-measuring-straight-line-distances.png)

*Using scale to measure a straight line*

- Measuring curved route distances:

  - Divide the route into segments
  - Rotate and mark the paper in stages to calculate the full distance
- Measuring road routes on the map:

  - Divide the route into straight sections using crosses
  - Use the paper to measure from A to the first cross
  - Rotate the paper, pivoting at the cross to mark the second cross

![Topographic map section showing a route marked in red through Filot, highlighting Croix de Berger, with contour lines and a river marked "Eau".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/4d9f130a7e24-measuring-curved-distances.png)

*Using scale to measure curved route distances*

## Area

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_6WyvDpmCSVgf9G6W` · Candidates should be able to: 
• select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols, a key, and other information 
• extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information presented on maps 
• use co-ordinates, latitude and longitude, 4 and 6 figure grid references 
• give directions using the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north 
• measure and estimate distances and area 
• use and interpret gradient, contour lines and spot heights; calculate differences in height 
• interpret cross-sections and transects.

## Area

- The scale of a map is important when accurately calculating area
- Areas can be divided into squares and triangles to make the calculation easier

  - The area of a rectangle = length x width
  - The area of a triangle = 1/2 base x height
- For a map with the scale 1:25,000
- To calculate an area where the length on the map is 4 cm and the width is 2 cm, the calculation is as follows:

  - Length 4 x 25,000 = 100,000 = 1,000 metres
  - Width 2 x 25,000 = 50,000 = 500 meters
- Area in m<sup>2 </sup>= 1000 x 500 = 500,000 meters<sup>2 </sup>or 0.5km<sup>2</sup>

## Bearings

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_ZKm5rbNWQVnT46Db` · Candidates should be able to: 
• select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols, a key, and other information 
• extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information presented on maps 
• use co-ordinates, latitude and longitude, 4 and 6 figure grid references 
• give directions using the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north 
• measure and estimate distances and area 
• use and interpret gradient, contour lines and spot heights; calculate differences in height 
• interpret cross-sections and transects.

## Bearings

- Directions on a map should always be given using compass points
- There are 16 compass points

![Compass rose diagram with sixteen cardinal and intercardinal points labelled: N, NNE, NE, ENE, E, ESE, SE, SSE, S, SSW, SW, WSW, W, WNW, NW, NNW.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/f6d1e3626b16-16-point-compass.png)

*Sixteen Compass Points*

- A grid bearing is measured from the grid north at 0°, east at 90°, south at 180°, and west at 270°
- Grid bearings are given using a protractor

  - The 0<sup>º</sup> should be pointing north and the centre of the protractor should be on the place the bearing is been given from
  - The compass direction and grid bearing from the crossroads at A to the location at B

![A topographical map featuring a protractor overlay with angles. Route A to B marked in red, highlighting locations and terrain features.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-geography-25/assets/5a4d113b4197-grid-bearings.png)

*Illustration showing how to take a map bearing*

- On the map below, B is south-west of A
- The bearing is 280<sup>º</sup>

## Height

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_s38rP4RvNt9GCYwh` · Candidates should be able to: 
• select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols, a key, and other information 
• extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information presented on maps 
• use co-ordinates, latitude and longitude, 4 and 6 figure grid references 
• give directions using the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north 
• measure and estimate distances and area 
• use and interpret gradient, contour lines and spot heights; calculate differences in height 
• interpret cross-sections and transects.

## Height

- There are three ways to display height:

  - **spot height**
  - **contour lines**
  - **trigonometrical (trig) stations**
- Spot heights show the height at a specific point with the height measurement written next to it
- Contour lines are** isolines**

  - They join points of **equal height **and are usually at 5 or 10-metre intervals (distance between the contour line)
  - This means that the height of the land increases by 5 or 10 metres between the lines
- A trigonometrical (trig) station is marked by a small black triangle with a height measurement written next to it

## Topography

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_vJXFyXCmq2fsf7Ff` · Candidates should be able to: 
• select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols, a key, and other information 
• extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information presented on maps 
• use co-ordinates, latitude and longitude, 4 and 6 figure grid references 
• give directions using the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north 
• measure and estimate distances and area 
• use and interpret gradient, contour lines and spot heights; calculate differences in height
